newsitem.title: USA: NYMEX crude ends sharply higher on Iraq tensions.
newsitem.headline: NYMEX crude ends sharply higher on Iraq tensions.

text.p: NYMEX oil prices rallied sharply Wednesday after bullish weather forecasts and political tensions in Iraq triggered heavy short covering in crude and heating oil.

"It was a real mixed bag of things. There was news Saddam Hussein put his wife under house arrest, you are two days before (Feb contract) expiration, and it's a bit chilly out there," said Mike DeLuca, trader with Prudential Securities.
After trading in tight range since Monday, Feb heat settled up 2.01 cents at 68.84 cents a gallon while March crude ended up 57 cents at $24.47 a barrel.
"A lot of shorts got spooked. You hit buy stops and before you knew it, you were up two cents in heat," said DeLuca.
The February refined product contract expires Friday, giving traders less time to cover their short positions in the prompt month.
Feb gasoline, finished up 1.19 cents at 68.23 cents a gallon, buoyed by heating oil.
The National Weather Service's six to 10 day forecast starting February 2 called for below normal temperatures throughout the key heating oil market of the northeastern United States.

On Tuesday, the American Petroleum Institute's (API) oil inventory data for the week ended January 24 said distillate stocks, comprised of heating oil and diesel, dropped 2.85 million barrels. Distillate demand was up 1.87 percent from a year ago.
Meanwhile, heightened tensions in Iraq sparked concerns about crude supplies in the Middle East Gulf.

The White House Press Secretary Mike McCurry, said on Wednesday that the White House sees internal "struggles for power" going on in Iraq for control. McCurry was commenting on reports by a senior U.S. military official that Iraqi President Saddam Hussein has put his wife under house arrest.
McCurry said the United States was "closely monitoring" the situation in Iraq.

Late Tuesday, a U.S. military official said Saddam's military forces had increased their training in recent weeks but there was no indication Iraq might repeat the attack on Kuwait that prompted the smashing of Saddam's forces by a U.S.-led military coalition in the 1991 Gulf War.
"The news got shorts panicked in crude," said a New York crude dealer.

Last December, the United Nations eased sanctions against Iraq and enabled Iraq to sell $2 billion worth of oil every six months, on a renewable basis, in exchange for humanitarian aid. The U.N. sanctions were imposed following Iraq's 1990 invasion of Kuwait.
((-- Harry Milling, New York Energy Desk, 212-859-1761))
